sections.heading: The question
sections.text: Ozone depletion — the destruction of the ozone layer caused by the presence of halocarbons, which were emitted from the late 1970s to the early 1990s<sup>1</sup> — has had far-reaching consequences for human health and ecosystems. sections.heading: The discovery
sections.text:
Observations alone cannot be used to directly assess the causality of the link between Arctic ozone depletion and surface climate. Moreover, because atmospheric conditions in the Arctic are subject to large interannual variations, the observational period (~40 years) is too short to draw a reliable conclusion. Therefore, in our study we used simulations with climate models that include atmospheric chemistry (chemistry–climate models). We used modelling approaches to artificially include and exclude the effects of ozone depletion on surface climate, thus we could isolate the effect of ozone depletion. We conducted model simulations over an extended time period (200 years) using current atmospheric conditions to obtain robust results.

By comparing model simulations that include and exclude ozone effects, we found that the influence of ozone depletion on Northern Hemisphere climate is larger than previously expected. Ozone depletion increases spring sea-level pressure anomalies over Eurasia by up to 3 hectopascal (hPa) compared with the results of simulations that exclude ozone effects, resulting in a warmer and drier climate across Europe (Fig1). Additionally, in seasons in which strong Arctic ozone depletion occurred springtime climate in the Northern Hemisphere can only be accurately reproduced by the models when ozone effects are included in the simulations. When the effects of ozone depletion are excluded, spring climate anomalies are underestimated by the models relative to the observed climate. These results therefore identify the lack of ozone effects in state-of-the-art forecast models of surface climate as a source of uncertainty in seasonal predictions.

![Figure 1](https://media.springernature.com/full/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41561-022-00983-6/MediaObjects/41561_2022_983_Fig1_HTML.png)

**Figure 1.** The effect of ozone depletion on the surface climate of the Northern Hemisphere.

Average deviation of the modelled surface temperature (a, c) and precipitation (b, d) from the spring climatologies of these variables in the 30 days after springtime Arctic ozone depletion in the 50 springs out of 200 with the most extreme ozone loss. Two models were used to perform the simulations, one with interactive ozone chemistry (INT-3D), which includes the effects of ozone on climate (a, b) and one with three-dimensional climatological ozone (CLIM-3D), which excludes such ozone effects (c, d). Stippling shows statistical significance on a 4.6% level following a bootstrapping test. © 2022, Friedel, M. et al.

sections.heading: The implications
sections.text:
The broader implications of our results are that information about the state of the ozone layer in the winter-to-spring season could potentially be used to improve weather predictions on sub-seasonal to seasonal timescales. For example, the probability of a wetter spring than usual may be higher for certain parts of Europe if Arctic ozone is depleted. Identifying ways to improve the accuracy of climate models has been a major challenge for researchers around the world. Current seasonal forecasting systems generally neglect the interactions between ozone and the atmospheric circulation. Therefore, these models may be missing an opportunity to increase the predictability of the climate in the Northern Hemisphere.

One of the limitations of our study is that the models we used have a crude representation of certain processes, for example micro-scale processes such as those involving clouds, and the underlying initial conditions for the simulations are not derived from real observations. Hence, the usability of our models for weather forecasting on sub-seasonal to seasonal time-scales is limited. Also, the amount of chemical ozone depletion simulated by our models may not be realistic. Hence, our research cannot say yet how predictable these depletion events are. However, our results highlight the potential to increase the accuracy of climate predictions beyond the limits of weather forecasting, by including the effects of ozone depletion in forecasting frameworks.

The next steps will involve using other climate models to assess how predictable these Arctic depletion events are (for example, how far in advance during the winter and spring season they can be predicted) and improve the ability of these modelling systems to represent the Arctic ozone.

Marina Friedel and Gabriel Chiodo

ETH Zürich, Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science, Zürich, Switzerland.

# Ozone depletion over the Arctic affects spring climate in the Northern Hemisphere

## The question

Ozone depletion — the destruction of the ozone layer caused by the presence of halocarbons, which were emitted from the late 1970s to the early 1990s<sup>1</sup> — has had far-reaching consequences for human health and ecosystems. Additionally, over Antarctica, where ozone depletion is greatest, the springtime formation of an ozone hole has led to climatic changes in the Southern Hemisphere<sup>2</sup>. Large-scale ozone depletion can also occur in the Northern Hemisphere; however, this occurs less frequently than in the Southern Hemisphere. A northern ozone depletion event was last observed in spring 2020<sup>3</sup>. Although such seasons of severe Arctic ozone depletion are typically followed by a warm and dry spring climate in Europe, ozone has not previously been considered an important factor in determining these climate patterns. Therefore, most seasonal forecasting systems do not consider the effect of ozone depletion on climate. Clarifying and quantifying the role of Arctic ozone depletion in determining the surface climate could reduce uncertainty in climate predictions.

## The discovery

Observations alone cannot be used to directly assess the causality of the link between Arctic ozone depletion and surface climate. Moreover, because atmospheric conditions in the Arctic are subject to large interannual variations, the observational period (~40 years) is too short to draw a reliable conclusion. Therefore, in our study we used simulations with climate models that include atmospheric chemistry (chemistry–climate models). We used modelling approaches to artificially include and exclude the effects of ozone depletion on surface climate, thus we could isolate the effect of ozone depletion. We conducted model simulations over an extended time period (200 years) using current atmospheric conditions to obtain robust results.

By comparing model simulations that include and exclude ozone effects, we found that the influence of ozone depletion on Northern Hemisphere climate is larger than previously expected. Ozone depletion increases spring sea-level pressure anomalies over Eurasia by up to 3 hectopascal (hPa) compared with the results of simulations that exclude ozone effects, resulting in a warmer and drier climate across Europe (Fig1). Additionally, in seasons in which strong Arctic ozone depletion occurred springtime climate in the Northern Hemisphere can only be accurately reproduced by the models when ozone effects are included in the simulations. When the effects of ozone depletion are excluded, spring climate anomalies are underestimated by the models relative to the observed climate. These results therefore identify the lack of ozone effects in state-of-the-art forecast models of surface climate as a source of uncertainty in seasonal predictions.

Average deviation of the modelled surface temperature (a, c) and precipitation (b, d) from the spring climatologies of these variables in the 30 days after springtime Arctic ozone depletion in the 50 springs out of 200 with the most extreme ozone loss. Two models were used to perform the simulations, one with interactive ozone chemistry (INT-3D), which includes the effects of ozone on climate (a, b) and one with three-dimensional climatological ozone (CLIM-3D), which excludes such ozone effects (c, d). Stippling shows statistical significance on a 4.6% level following a bootstrapping test. © 2022, Friedel, M. et al.

## The implications

The broader implications of our results are that information about the state of the ozone layer in the winter-to-spring season could potentially be used to improve weather predictions on sub-seasonal to seasonal timescales. For example, the probability of a wetter spring than usual may be higher for certain parts of Europe if Arctic ozone is depleted. Identifying ways to improve the accuracy of climate models has been a major challenge for researchers around the world. Current seasonal forecasting systems generally neglect the interactions between ozone and the atmospheric circulation. Therefore, these models may be missing an opportunity to increase the predictability of the climate in the Northern Hemisphere.

One of the limitations of our study is that the models we used have a crude representation of certain processes, for example micro-scale processes such as those involving clouds, and the underlying initial conditions for the simulations are not derived from real observations. Hence, the usability of our models for weather forecasting on sub-seasonal to seasonal time-scales is limited. Also, the amount of chemical ozone depletion simulated by our models may not be realistic. Hence, our research cannot say yet how predictable these depletion events are. However, our results highlight the potential to increase the accuracy of climate predictions beyond the limits of weather forecasting, by including the effects of ozone depletion in forecasting frameworks.

The next steps will involve using other climate models to assess how predictable these Arctic depletion events are (for example, how far in advance during the winter and spring season they can be predicted) and improve the ability of these modelling systems to represent the Arctic ozone.

Marina Friedel and Gabriel Chiodo

ETH Zürich, Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science, Zürich, Switzerland.

## Expert opinion

“This research is novel because it dismisses an alternative hypothesis that large ozone loss simply coincides with a strong Arctic Oscillation state. This study suggests that including interactive ozone chemistry in seasonal-prediction models would improve the predictability of the Arctic Oscillation on timescales of up to two months, which would be of considerable societal benefit.” Olaf Morgenstern, National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research, Wellington, New Zealand

## Behind the paper

Research on the link between Arctic ozone and climate began in 2011, when one of the most extreme ozone depletions occurred. Studies with conflicting conclusions motivated G.C. to write a proposal, which was later funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation. The common view was that Arctic ozone depletion was driven by special meteorological conditions, such as a cold polar stratosphere. As ozone and meteorology are closely intertwined, it is difficult to assess causality: we wanted to overcome this limitation by combining observations and complex model calculations. We started this endeavour in 2019, but difficulties in the implementation led us to the idea of using a hybrid configuration, allowing meteorological conditions to affect ozone; this was crucial for isolating the effects of ozone. With these new results, we hope to pave the way for improvements in the representation of ozone in weather models. G.C. and M.F.

## From the editor

“Friedel et al. show for the first time how the continued emission of ozone-destroying chemicals can perturb climate patterns across the Northern Hemisphere. Their innovative atmospheric chemistry modelling also opens up intriguing ways to improve temperature and precipitation predictions months into the future.” James Super, Senior Editor, Nature Geoscience.
